A: Typeface guidance stays generic ('a neutral sans of the Helvetica/Inter class') where concrete, vettable families would make the spec directly executable
Prose is dense and occasionally rhetorical ('scarcity economics', 'trend trap'), spending words that a spec reader must unpack
Accessibility section omits text-zoom/reflow and colour-vision-deficiency simulation, both relevant to the stated 60+ audience
B: No token/design-system governance story: nothing ensures the restraint and the two-family budget survive future contributors
The supporting influence's boundary is looser than A's - no explicit rule for what classical print may NOT do when it conflicts with clarity
Chart integrity is thinner (palette ramp specified, but no guidance on axis honesty, baselines, or stale-data handling for figures the bank is accountable for)

notes: Both teams converged on Swiss/International Typographic primary with a print/editorial supporting voice, satisfied every brief element within the line limit, and named a fashionable-but-unsuitable rejection (glassmorphism). B is the more immediately buildable spec (named fonts, hex values, row heights, max widths, print stylesheet, CVD simulation). A wins narrowly on depth of reasoning: an explicitly budgeted supporting influence with a conflict rule, semantic-colour reservation argued from instrumentation practice, chart honesty and data-recency rules, and a governance/token layer that makes the restraint durable - the quality that matters most for a regulated bank's decade-scale system.
